label: Ireland

allocation.label: Single transferable vote (regional seat curve, transfers folded in)

governmentText.majority: {party} governs alone with {seats} seats, something no party has managed in the Dáil since 1977.
governmentText.coalition: {parties} agree a programme for government ({seats} seats), and the Taoiseach's chair goes to the larger party.
governmentText.confidence_supply: {lead} governs as a minority with confidence and supply from {partner}, the arrangement Fine Gael and Fianna Fáil used from 2016.
governmentText.minority: {party} leads a minority government on {seats} seats and leans on the independents, as Irish governments so often do.
governmentText.hung: No combination reaches a majority. {largest} is the largest party, and the talks run on for weeks.

goalHint: Reach {majority} of {total} seats, alone or with partners. Seats follow first preferences region by region, and independents hold a large block you cannot lead but can court. Fianna Fáil and Fine Gael can pair up, but neither will touch Sinn Féin.

issues.name: The bailout & the banks
issues.blurb: The bank guarantee, the Troika deal and who pays for both.

issues.name: Cost of living
issues.blurb: Energy bills, groceries and the price of nearly everything.

issues.name: Housing
issues.blurb: Rents, mortgages, homelessness and a country that does not build enough.

issues.name: Health service
issues.blurb: Trolleys, waiting lists and a system that never quite gets fixed.

issues.name: Tax & public spending
issues.blurb: Austerity, the universal social charge and what a surplus is for.

issues.name: Water charges
issues.blurb: Irish Water, the meters and the biggest protests in a generation.

issues.name: Political reform
issues.blurb: A smaller Dáil, no Seanad and cleaner politics after the crash.

issues.name: The border & Irish unity
issues.blurb: Northern Ireland, the border and the case for a united Ireland.

issues.name: Climate & environment
issues.blurb: Emission targets, the farm lobby and the cost of going green.

issues.name: Immigration
issues.blurb: Asylum numbers, accommodation and the limits of public patience.

regions.name: Rest of Munster (Kerry, Limerick, Clare, Tipperary)

2007.label: 2007 · Ahern v. Kenny
2007.tagline: May 2007. Bertie Ahern is after a third term at the head of a Fianna Fáil and Progressive Democrat government. Enda Kenny's Fine Gael and Pat Rabbitte's Labour offer an 'Alliance for Change' with an agreed transfer pact, and questions about the Taoiseach's finances at the Mahon Tribunal dominate the first fortnight. The polls say it could go either way. Win the most seats, then find the numbers.

events.headline: Ahern calls the election early on Sunday 29 April, and evidence about his finances in 1994 that has just leaked to the Mahon Tribunal dominates the first fortnight. {party} fights on the defensive
Ahern stands with Tony Blair at Stormont on 8 May as Ian Paisley and Martin McGuinness take office, and {party} goes into the last fortnight as the party of the peace process
Ahern becomes the first Irish Taoiseach to address both Houses of the British Parliament on 15 May, in the middle of the campaign, and {party} has a statesman's stage
The Prime Time debate between Ahern and Kenny concentrates on Kenny's lack of experience, and an Irish Times poll in the last week has {party} back at 41%
Fine Gael's Contract for a Better Ireland is the centrepiece of its campaign, with set totals of hospital beds, gardaí and teachers, and {party} says it is the government that is not delivering
Fine Gael and Labour offer the Alliance for Change, a proposed coalition with an agreed transfer pact, and {party} says only a change of government will fix health and crime
The Progressive Democrats decide to stay in government rather than pull out over Ahern's finances, and {party}'s partners have bought the Taoiseach his time
Finance Minister Brian Cowen's robust exchanges in the final stretch rally the party's base, and {party} has an asset on the stump
The Greens stay non-aligned but say they favour a change from the outgoing government, and {party} is the only party willing to talk to Sinn Féin
Every party except the Greens says it would not put Sinn Féin in a government, and {party} fights for its seats from outside the pacts
Early polls show the Alliance for Change gaining on the government, and some commentators say Fianna Fáil could come back with only 65 seats. {party} warns its voters not to stay at home

issues.name: Health
issues.blurb: Trolleys in hospital corridors and the parties' promises of so many more hospital beds.

issues.name: Crime
issues.blurb: Gang violence and the parties' promises of so many more gardaí.

issues.name: The economy
issues.blurb: A long boom, rising house prices and the question of who can keep it going.

issues.name: Ahern & the Mahon Tribunal
issues.blurb: Evidence about the Taoiseach's finances in 1994, and whether he is fit to serve.

issues.name: Education
issues.blurb: Class sizes and the parties' promises on pupil-teacher ratios.

issues.name: Alliance for Change
issues.blurb: Fine Gael and Labour's pre-election pact against the Fianna Fáil and Progressive Democrat government.

2011.label: 2011 · Kenny v. Gilmore v. Martin
2011.tagline: February 2011. The Troika has arrived, Brian Cowen is gone, the Greens have walked out and Fianna Fáil is about to be wiped off the map. Fine Gael and Labour are fighting to be the senior partner in a coalition nobody doubts. Win 84 seats, or at least be in the room.

events.headline: Cowen quits as Fianna Fáil leader after a botched reshuffle and the Greens walk out of government. Micheál Martin inherits the party, and the blame lands on {party}
Gilmore calls the Troika deal a bad deal and says it is 'Frankfurt's way or Labour's way'. The crowds cheer, the economists wince, and {party} has to explain how
Enda Kenny turns down the TV3 leaders' debate, and Fianna Fáil and Labour say {party} is running scared
Kenny is photographed with Angela Merkel in Berlin, and {party} looks like a government in waiting
A private poll puts Labour on 16 per cent, it drops talk of 'Gilmore for Taoiseach', and its 'Every Little Hurts' ads put {party}'s tax and spending plans on the defensive
Kenny's performance in the final Prime Time debate is judged a disappointment, and talk of an overall majority for {party} fades
Gerry Adams leaves Belfast to stand in Louth, and Sinn Féin's 'There is a Better Way' picks up the protest votes angry about the bailout, to the benefit of {party}
The United Left Alliance's anti-austerity message cuts through in working-class Dublin, and {party} puts a few extra candidates in play
Garret FitzGerald urges a Fine Gael and Labour coalition and warns against one-party government, and {party} picks up late tactical votes
Micheál Martin's calm showings in the television debates win some friendly reviews, and {party} stops sinking in the polls
The Greens run a clean-up-the-mess campaign on climate and reform, but voters remember the bank guarantee, and {party} fights for a single seat
Local independents with a record of constituency work stand against the discredited party machines, and {party} draws votes in the towns

issues.name: The bailout & the banks
issues.blurb: The €85 billion EU-IMF deal, the 2008 bank guarantee, and whether to burn the bondholders.

issues.name: Austerity
issues.blurb: €15 billion of cuts and tax rises planned to 2014: how fast, and who would bear them.

issues.name: Jobs & emigration
issues.blurb: Unemployment above 14%, and young people leaving again for Australia, Canada and Britain.

issues.name: Political reform
issues.blurb: Abolishing the Seanad, a smaller Dáil, and an end to the politics that led to the crash.

issues.name: Health service
issues.blurb: Trolleys, two-tier access, and Fine Gael's plan for universal health insurance.

issues.name: Pay & household bills
issues.blurb: Pay cuts, the new universal social charge on every payslip, and rising household bills.

issues.name: Mortgages & ghost estates
issues.blurb: Homeowners in negative equity and arrears after the property crash, and empty ghost estates.

2016.label: 2016 · Kenny v. Martin
2016.tagline: February 2016. Fine Gael and Labour ask to be kept on to finish the recovery. Water charges, homelessness and a rural revolt are splitting the vote five ways and independents are multiplying. A government with a majority is not on the cards, so the question is who ends up propping up whom.

events.headline: Enda Kenny names 26 February on Twitter while driving to the Áras to dissolve the Dáil and asks the country to keep the recovery going, and {party} owns the early running
Fianna Fáil promises to suspend water charges and wind up Irish Water, and {party} finally has a mainstream home for the protest vote
The High Court rejects the Greens' bid to put Eamon Ryan in the RTÉ leaders' debate, and {party}, with no TDs, struggles for airtime
A bidding war over the universal social charge has Fine Gael promising to scrap it and Fianna Fáil promising deep cuts, and {party} struggles to be heard
Poll after poll shows the lead slipping, as voters who do not feel the recovery tell the doorstep so, and {party} watches the numbers fall
Kenny faces Martin, Burton and Adams in the final RTÉ leaders' debate three days before polling, and {party} carries the recovery argument into the last week
A Right2Change pact asks left voters to give their transfers to each other, and {party} hopes the water protests turn into seats
Fine Gael and Fianna Fáil both rule out governing with Sinn Féin, and {party} says it is for the voters to decide
A record number of families in emergency accommodation makes housing the question the coalition cannot answer, and {party} picks up the anger
The Independent Alliance publishes its charter for government and rural independents become the kingmakers everyone is counting, with {party} drawing the votes
The new Social Democrats publish a ten-year plan, Building a Better Future, and {party} starts picking up the professional vote
Micheál Martin's calm tour of the south and east steadies the party after the wipeout, and {party} comes back from the dead

issues.name: Water charges
issues.blurb: Irish Water, the bills and the Right2Water protests, with Fianna Fáil now promising to suspend charges.

issues.name: Health service
issues.blurb: Record trolley numbers in A&E, long waiting lists, and the shelved plan for universal health insurance.

issues.name: Homelessness & rents
issues.blurb: Families in hotel rooms, Dublin rents rising about 10% a year, and too few houses being built.

issues.name: The recovery & the USC
issues.blurb: How to use the 'fiscal space', cuts to the universal social charge, and 'keep the recovery going'.

issues.name: Cost of living
issues.blurb: Childcare, insurance and household charges after years of austerity.

issues.name: Political reform
issues.blurb: Promises of Dáil reform after a government with a huge majority that guillotined its bills.

2020.label: 2020 · Varadkar v. Martin v. McDonald
2020.tagline: February 2020. Fine Gael has governed for nine years on a recovering economy and a Brexit deal, and the voters on trolleys and on rent have noticed. Sinn Féin is rising on housing with too few candidates to turn it all into seats. A three-way split is coming and the Greens are in the mix.

events.headline: Leo Varadkar calls the first Saturday election since 1918 and runs on Brexit and a recovering economy, and {party} presents itself as the steady hand
Housing is the first issue on every doorstep, and {party}, in office through years of rent rises, takes the heat
A poll puts Sinn Féin ahead of both Fianna Fáil and Fine Gael. The party is running too few candidates to cash it in, but {party} has the momentum
RTÉ invites Mary Lou McDonald into the final leaders' debate after Sinn Féin threatens legal action, and {party} gets the stage it wanted
Micheál Martin and Leo Varadkar both rule out governing with Sinn Féin, and {party} says the voters, not the two old parties, will decide
Fianna Fáil, which expected to be the largest party, finds the cities slipping away to Sinn Féin, and {party} watches the transfers drain
The Greens ride a strong run in the 2019 local and European elections into the campaign, and {party} aims for its best result ever
Aontú, founded by Peadar Tóibín after he left Sinn Féin over abortion, contests its first general election and {party} courts the rural vote
Another record trolley count in the hospitals ends the government's talk of a health service on the mend, and {party} wears it
The Social Democrats, deliberately running a short list in winnable seats, put their effort where it counts, and {party} is the beneficiary
Fianna Fáil asks voters to let it end the confidence and supply deal it signed with Fine Gael in 2016 and lead the next government, and {party} runs as the party of change from inside the system

issues.name: Housing & rents
issues.blurb: Record rents, about 10,000 people in emergency accommodation, and young people unable to buy.

issues.name: Health
issues.blurb: Record trolley numbers, long waiting lists and the overspend on the new National Children's Hospital.

issues.name: Pension age
issues.blurb: The State pension age rising to 67 in 2021, leaving people who retire at 65 on jobseeker's benefit.

issues.name: Brexit & the border
issues.blurb: The UK's exit on 31 January, the Northern Ireland protocol, and Sinn Féin's push for a border poll.

issues.name: Cost of living
issues.blurb: Childcare costs, and insurance premiums that kept rising for motorists and businesses.

issues.name: Climate action
issues.blurb: The carbon tax raised to €26 a tonne, and the Greens' call to cut emissions by 7% a year.

issues.name: Tax & spending
issues.blurb: Fine Gael's USC cuts, against Sinn Féin plans to tax high earners and abolish the property tax.

2024.label: 2024 · Harris v. Martin v. McDonald
2024.tagline: November 2024. Fianna Fáil, Fine Gael and the Greens go to the country after a giveaway budget and a new Taoiseach in Simon Harris. Sinn Féin led the polls through the housing crisis and has slipped since. Nobody is close to 88 seats, so the independents and the transfers decide it.

events.headline: Simon Harris calls a 29 November election seven months after becoming Taoiseach, on the back of a budget full of giveaways. {party} goes in with a spring in its step
Michael O'Leary tells a Fine Gael candidate's launch there are too many former teachers in the Dáil. The unions take offence, and {party} wishes it had never handed him a microphone
RTÉ stages the biggest leaders' debate in Irish history, with ten party leaders on one stage, and {party} gets airtime it could never buy
Sinn Féin's manifesto promises a review of RTÉ's news coverage. Rivals call it a threat to press freedom, and {party} spends two days on the defensive
Harris walks away from a disability carer in Kanturk who accuses the government of neglecting her sector. The video runs all weekend and {party} has a problem
Independent Ireland's Dublin South-Central candidate resigns from the party after a row over his association with Conor McGregor, and {party} spends the final weekend explaining itself
The government's €14 billion Apple tax windfall becomes a campaign question. {party} says it should build homes and fix hospitals now, not sit in a fund
Immigration climbs the agenda, with calls for tighter controls and stiffer asylum rules, and {party} finds an audience
Voters who backed the Greens to get climate action remember who raised the carbon tax, and {party} fights for a single seat
Holly Cairns campaigns while heavily pregnant and moves to social media for the last week, and {party} wins a warm round of coverage
Ivana Bacik pitches Labour as the partner for a left-of-centre bloc, and {party} gets a second look from voters who are tired of both big parties
A pledge to abolish stamp duty for first-time buyers on homes under €450,000 keeps the housing debate on young buyers, and {party} gains with the young

issues.name: Housing
issues.blurb: Rents, over 14,000 people in emergency accommodation, and rival targets for homes built each year.

issues.name: Cost of living
issues.blurb: Energy bills, childcare and grocery prices, after a budget of once-off payments and credits.

issues.name: Health
issues.blurb: Trolley counts, waiting lists, and services for children with disabilities.

issues.name: Immigration
issues.blurb: Asylum seekers sleeping rough, protests at sites such as Coolock, and calls for tighter controls.

issues.name: The Apple money
issues.blurb: What to do with €14 billion from the Apple tax ruling, and how to spend a large budget surplus.

issues.name: Climate
issues.blurb: The carbon tax, retrofit grants, and whether the Greens' climate targets would survive them.

events.headline: Grim figures on the live register lead the news, putting pressure on {party}
Another record rent rise puts housing on the front page, and voters look to {party}
{party}'s leader wins the televised leaders' debate, and the Twitter poll agrees
A candidate's old social media posts resurface, and {party} spends the day apologising
Voters are urged to number every candidate on the ballot, and the transfers drift toward {party}
{party}'s leader fumbles a costings question on Morning Ireland
The Sunday papers and a handful of business groups line up behind {party}
A viral clip breaks for {party} among first-time voters
A bus tour of the county towns wins {party} friendly local coverage and a few local radio hits
A winter storm knocks out power across the west and puts leadership first, and {party} looks the part
RTÉ offers {party} a slot in a prime-time leaders' debate
events.prompt: A prime-time debate is on the table. How do you play it?

choices.text: Accept and go on the attack
choices.resultText: You land blows and take a few. The overnight polls twitch your way.
A steady, on-message night. No gaffes, no fireworks.
You dodge the studio lights. The papers call it running scared.

events.headline: Every doorstep asks {party} the same question: who gets your second preferences?
events.prompt: Voters want to know where your transfers go. What do you tell them?

choices.text: Name your preferred partners and say so on every ballot leaflet
choices.resultText: Clarity reassures your side. The other side calls it a stitch-up.

choices.text: Tell supporters to number down the ballot and say nothing more
choices.resultText: Nobody is ruled out, and nobody is quite reassured.

choices.text: Rule out the main rival and dare voters to choose
choices.resultText: A bold line. It sharpens the contrast and costs you a few transfers.

events.headline: {party}'s front bench is split on the headline manifesto pledge
events.prompt: The manifesto goes to print on Friday. Which way do you push?

choices.text: Go bold with a defining, risky pledge
choices.resultText: The base roars. The Department of Finance starts sharpening pencils.

choices.text: Play it safe: no hostages to fortune
Make it a contrast with the rival's costings
choices.resultText: You define them more than yourself, and it lands.
